explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Solomon, Israel's king, says it to the LORD: “But I have built You an exalted house, a place for You to dwell forever.” An exalted house, a place to dwell forever: that's exactly how he puts it.

Not this time, friend. Solomon, Israel's king, does say it, and he says it to the LORD: “But I have built You an exalted house, a place for You to dwell forever.” I spent years in the back of a junk drawer, so a house to dwell in forever sounds mighty fancy to me.

Yes, baker! Solomon, Israel's king, says the LORD spoke this promise “…to my father David…” So Solomon is standing inside a promise his own dad received, and the LORD fulfilled it with His own hand. The promise was spoken, and now it's built.

Good guess, friend. Moses, Israel's leader, heard plenty from God (Exodus 20:1). But Solomon, Israel's king, names a different person here: “…my father David…” The promise about the house was spoken to David.

Close to the right neighborhood, baker, but not the right person. Abraham heard from God long before this (Genesis 12:1). Solomon, Israel's king, says the promise was spoken “…to my father David…” David is the one who heard it.

Jerusalem it is, friend! The LORD says, “But now I have chosen Jerusalem for My Name to be there, and I have chosen David to be over My people Israel.” A city and a king, chosen side by side. Before that, He hadn't chosen any city from any tribe.

Hebron is a fair guess, baker, but it's not the city here. The LORD says that since the day He brought His people out of Egypt, He hadn't chosen a city from any tribe for His Name. Then comes “But now I have chosen Jerusalem for My Name to be there…” Jerusalem is the one.

Shiloh is a fair guess, friend, but the LORD names a different city. He says He hadn't chosen a city from any tribe for His Name, and then He says, “But now I have chosen Jerusalem for My Name to be there…” So the blank belongs to Jerusalem. David gets named right alongside it.

explanations.answer: He did well to have it in his heart
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The LORD tells David, “…you have done well to have this in your heart.” David wasn't going to be the builder, but the LORD still praised the desire. I've had plenty of plans in my heart that never made it out of the dough, so I love that.

explanations.answer: He should have asked a prophet first
explanations.explanation: No prophet comes into it, friend. The LORD says to David, “…you have done well to have this in your heart.” That's praise, plain and simple.

explanations.answer: He was reaching too high for a king
explanations.explanation: No scolding anywhere in this one, baker. The LORD tells David, “…you have done well to have this in your heart.” If a king can't dream big, who can? The LORD called it done well.

Careful, friend, because it's the other way around. The LORD tells David, “Nevertheless, you are not the one to build it; but your son, your own offspring, will build the house for My Name.” David is not the builder. His son is.

Right, baker. The LORD says to David, “…you are not the one to build it; but your son, your own offspring, will build the house for My Name.” David had the idea, and his own son gets the job. The word “Nevertheless” is the turn in that sentence.

explanations.answer: The ark holding the LORD's covenant
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend! Solomon says, “And there I have placed the ark, which contains the covenant of the LORD that He made with the children of Israel.” The ark is the thing he places in the house. And the ark contains the covenant of the LORD.
Good memory, baker. Moses, Israel's leader, did make a bronze snake (Numbers 21:9). But that's not what Solomon names here. He says he placed the ark, “…which contains the covenant of the LORD…”

explanations.answer: The sword that belonged to Goliath
explanations.explanation: Goliath's sword does turn up in David's story, friend. David used it to finish the fight with the giant (1 Samuel 17:51). But Solomon doesn't mention it here. What he places in the house is the ark, which contains the covenant of the LORD.

explanations.answer: Kneels and spreads his hands toward heaven
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. On the platform, Solomon “…knelt down before the whole assembly of Israel, spread out his hands toward heaven…” The king gets down on his knees in front of everyone. I think that tells you where his heart is.

explanations.answer: Reads the law of Moses out loud
explanations.explanation: Good thought, friend, but the text has something else. Up on the platform, Solomon “…knelt down before the whole assembly of Israel, spread out his hands toward heaven…” Then he prays. Reading aloud isn't mentioned.

explanations.answer: Holds up the tablets for all to see
explanations.explanation: No tablets in this scene, baker. The text says he “…knelt down before the whole assembly of Israel, spread out his hands toward heaven…” After that, he starts to pray. Kneeling and open hands are what the whole crowd sees.

Careful, friend, it's the opposite. Solomon prays, “O LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like You in heaven or on earth…” He isn't saying other gods match the LORD. He's saying there is no God like Him.

Right, baker. Solomon starts with “O LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like You in heaven or on earth…” No other gods get a mention. The prayer starts with who the LORD is, and the covenant He keeps comes right after.

That's it, friend! The promise comes “…if only your descendants guard their way to walk in My law as you have walked before Me.” The word is law. The throne promise comes with the condition of walking in it.

Good try, baker, since a house is all over this chapter. But the if in the promise is about walking in the LORD's law. The text says, “…if only your descendants guard their way to walk in My law as you have walked before Me.”

Land is a fair guess, friend, since Solomon talks about it later. But in this promise, the if is about walking in the LORD's law. The words are “…guard their way to walk in My law as you have walked before Me.”

Yes, baker! Solomon says, “The heavens, even the highest heavens, cannot contain You, much less this temple I have built.” If the highest heavens can't contain God, then this temple can't either. That's how Solomon puts it.

No seas in this prayer, friend, so you can put the swim trunks away. Solomon says, “The heavens, even the highest heavens, cannot contain You, much less this temple I have built.” He looks up to the highest heavens, not down to the seas.
Deserts aren't in this part of the prayer, baker. Solomon says, “The heavens, even the highest heavens, cannot contain You, much less this temple I have built.” He's looking up, not out.
That's right, friend. Solomon prays, “May Your eyes be open toward this temple day and night…” Day and night, no breaks. He asks the LORD to hear the prayer prayed toward that place.

It's true, baker. Solomon prays, “May Your eyes be open toward this temple day and night, toward the place where You said You would put Your Name…” Day and night, he asks. That includes the nights when I'm asleep on the counter.

Yes, baker! Solomon asks, “May You hear from heaven, Your dwelling place.” Israel prays toward the temple, and Solomon asks the LORD to hear from heaven. It matches what he said about the highest heavens.
Good guess, friend, but it isn't the words in the prayer. Solomon says, “May You hear from heaven, Your dwelling place.” The people pray toward this place. The LORD hears from heaven.

explanations.answer: From the top of Mount Zion
explanations.explanation: Nice try, baker, but Solomon doesn't name a mountain here. He asks, “May You hear from heaven, Your dwelling place.” The place he names is heaven, not a mountain.
That's the word, friend! Solomon prays, “May You hear and forgive.” Hear, then forgive. I'd like both of those on every day of my life.
Counting never comes up in this prayer, baker. Solomon says, “May You hear and forgive.” Hear first, and then forgive.
No testing in this part, friend. Solomon says, “May You hear and forgive.” He asks for forgiveness right after hearing.

Yes, friend, wicked goes in the first blank. Solomon asks the LORD to judge, “…condemning the wicked man by bringing down on his own head what he has done…” What he did comes back on his own head. That's the first half of the judgment.

Right, baker, righteous goes in the second blank. Solomon asks God to be “…justifying the righteous man by rewarding him according to his righteousness.” So the judgment goes both ways. The righteous man gets rewarded.
Money doesn't come into this one, friend. Solomon's two men are the wicked man and the righteous man. His request is about what each one has done.

A foreigner does show up later in the prayer, baker (2 Chronicles 6:32), but that's a separate case. Here, Solomon is talking about a man who is required to take an oath before the altar. He asks God to condemn the wicked man and justify the righteous man.
Being poor isn't part of this one, friend. Solomon says the judgment is about the wicked man and the righteous man. What matters is what each one has done.
That's right, baker. Solomon says Israel is defeated “…because they have sinned against You…” He names the reason out loud. Then he says they return, confess God's name, and pray in the temple.

explanations.answer: Their army has grown too small
explanations.explanation: Army size isn't mentioned, friend. Solomon says Israel is defeated “…because they have sinned against You…” The reason he gives is sin. Then he asks what should happen when they return.

explanations.answer: Their king has grown too proud
explanations.explanation: Pride isn't mentioned in this verse, baker. Solomon says Israel is defeated “…because they have sinned against You…” That's the reason he gives, and he says it plainly.

Careful, friend, because the land isn't brand new. Solomon asks God to forgive them and says, “May You restore them to the land You gave to them and their fathers.” He asks for the land God already gave them. Restoring is a different thing than something new.

Right, baker. Solomon asks God to hear from heaven and forgive, then says, “May You restore them to the land You gave to them and their fathers.” It's the same land, not a new one. Forgiveness comes first, and then the restoring.

explanations.answer: The good way they should walk
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend! Solomon asks God to forgive them “…so that You may teach them the good way in which they should walk.” Both are requests: forgive and teach. After that, he asks God to send rain on the land.

explanations.answer: How to store water for dry years
explanations.explanation: Smart idea, baker, but it isn't in the prayer. Solomon asks for forgiveness “…so that You may teach them the good way in which they should walk.” The teaching is about the way they walk. The rain is a separate request.
Planting isn't mentioned, friend. Solomon says, “…so that You may teach them the good way in which they should walk.” The teaching is about how they walk. The rain comes in his next request.
That's the word, baker! Solomon says, “…You alone know the hearts of men…” Only God knows what's in every heart. That's why he asks Him to forgive and repay each man.
Names don't come up here, friend. Solomon says, “…You alone know the hearts of men…” That's the word that fits the blank. God sees what's inside.

Homes aren't mentioned in this part, baker. Solomon says, “…You alone know the hearts of men…” God knows the heart of each man. That's why he asks God to forgive and repay each man according to his ways.

explanations.answer: All peoples will know His name and fear Him
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend! Solomon says, “Then all the peoples of the earth will know Your name and fear You, as do Your people Israel…” It's the whole world, not just Israel. They'll know the house is called by God's Name too.

explanations.answer: The foreigner will bring the temple rich gifts
explanations.explanation: Gifts aren't mentioned here, baker. Solomon says, “Then all the peoples of the earth will know Your name and fear You, as do Your people Israel…” The result he names is that people everywhere know God's name.

explanations.answer: Israel's enemies will all be put to shame
explanations.explanation: Shame isn't what he asks for here, friend. Solomon says, “Then all the peoples of the earth will know Your name and fear You, as do Your people Israel…” The result is that all peoples know God's name.

That's right, baker. Solomon asks, “…then may You hear from heaven their prayer and their plea, and may You uphold their cause.” They pray toward the city and the temple, and he asks God to hear from heaven. He asks God to uphold their cause.

Actually it's true, friend. Solomon asks, “…then may You hear from heaven their prayer and their plea, and may You uphold their cause.” (2 Chronicles 6:35) When Israel goes to war and prays toward the city and the temple, that's what he asks. "False" looked tempting, but I've stared at dough for years thinking it was ready, so you're in good company.

Yes, baker. Solomon pictures an enemy “…who takes them as captives to a land far or near…” That's a heavy picture. I think it makes the next part, where they come to their senses and return, matter even more.
It isn't soldiers, friend. Solomon says the enemy “…takes them as captives to a land far or near…” It's a heavy picture, so the text is plain about it.
Guests is a long way off, baker. Solomon says the enemy “…takes them as captives to a land far or near…” That's a heavy picture, and the word is captives.

That's right, friend. Solomon says that in the land of their enemies, when they return to God with all their heart and soul, they pray “…in the direction of the land that You gave to their fathers, the city You have chosen, and the house I have built for Your Name…” Even from far away, their prayer is aimed at those places.

It's true, baker. Solomon says, “…when they pray in the direction of the land that You gave to their fathers, the city You have chosen, and the house I have built for Your Name…” This is what the captives do, in the land of the enemies who took them. Then Solomon asks God to hear from heaven.
That's it, friend! Solomon prays, “Now therefore, arise, O LORD God, and enter Your resting place, You and the ark of Your might.” The ark goes in with Him. It's a big way to close out the prayer.

Close in spirit, baker, but it's not the words Solomon uses. He prays, “…arise, O LORD God, and enter Your resting place, You and the ark of Your might.” The answer is a resting place. The ark is mentioned right alongside Him.
A city comes up earlier in the prayer, friend, but not here. Solomon says, “…arise, O LORD God, and enter Your resting place, You and the ark of Your might.” The answer is His resting place.
